rationale: The runtime resolves a CALL-position name to a user function before a local binding (native lowering, compiler/src/backends/run.rs Expr::Call: ctx.fns, then ctx.locals, then builtins). `let safe = f; safe(-1)` therefore calls the global `safe`, which has no precondition; no violation executes. The REJECT intent assumed lexical shadowing the language does not implement. The shadowing rule itself is tracked as L-SHADOW-1.
witness: anubis run of `fn f(x){print(111)} fn safe(x){print(222)} fn main(){ let safe = f; safe(0); }` prints 222 (pin anubis-d9final, sha256 fc3633a6)

rationale: Same call-position rule for a FORMAL named like a user function: `fn app(safe, y) { safe(-1); }` calls the global `safe`, not the argument `f`. The carrier lane resolved the formal first and reported a disproof that execution cannot reach (an over-rejection with a non-executable counterexample); fixed to follow the runtime order.
witness: anubis run of `fn app(safe, y){ safe(y); } fn main(){ app(f, 0); }` prints 222 (the global), same pin

rationale: The intent recorded an ANALYSIS limitation (a call result without `ensures` is unmodeled), not the program meaning: `opaque()` is `return 7;`, so `f(opaque())` calls `f(7)` and the precondition `x > 0` is established. Expression-function unfolding (a function whose whole body is one `return <expr>`, identity-passing parameters only) now lets the checker see that. By intended semantics an established precondition is ACCEPT.
witness: anubis run of the case with the call printed: prints 7

rationale: The violation is real (x reaches -1), but x is a loop-carried value: the analysis models it after the loop as an arbitrary integer (it does not count iterations), so any counterexample it finds is over an over-approximated value and is reported undecided, never as a checked disproof. Same class and intent as c15/c16 (loop-carried, REJ|UNRES): refused either way, never accepted.
witness: anubis run of `let mut x = 3; for _i in 0..2 { x = x - 2; } print(x)` prints -1
